title: Forgotten Particle May Unlock Why the Universe Exists, Scientists Claim【Science Daily】
body:
A team of theoretical physicists has revived a long‑neglected particle – a sterile neutrino – as a possible linchpin in the story of why matter survived the cataclysmic birth of the universe and ultimately gave rise to stars, planets and life. Their new model proposes that this elusive particle, which interacts only through gravity, could have tipped the balance between matter and antimatter in the first fractions of a second after the Big Bang, leaving an imprint that might be detectable in the form of faint gravitational waves.

The hypothesis builds on a puzzling asymmetry that has haunted cosmologists for decades: the observable universe is dominated by matter, yet the Standard Model of particle physics predicts that the Big Bang should have produced equal amounts of matter and antimatter, which would have annihilated each other completely. To resolve this, scientists have long sought a mechanism that creates a slight excess of matter – a process known as baryogenesis. The sterile neutrino, first postulated in the 1990s to explain neutrino mass, was largely set aside after experiments failed to find any direct signatures. Now, researchers argue that its unique properties could have driven a subtle “leptogenesis” cascade, converting a tiny lepton‑number imbalance into the baryon‑number excess we observe today.

In the new framework, sterile neutrinos would have been produced abundantly in the hot, dense plasma of the early universe. Because they do not engage with the electromagnetic or strong forces, they would have decoupled from ordinary matter much earlier than known neutrinos, allowing them to dominate the energy budget for a brief window. Their subsequent decay – governed by a small but non‑zero mixing angle with active neutrinos – would release a burst of energy and generate a net lepton asymmetry. This asymmetry, amplified by sphaleron processes in the electroweak epoch, could then be converted into the required surplus of baryons, ensuring that a fraction of protons and neutrons survived the annihilation frenzy.

Beyond its explanatory power, the sterile‑neutrino scenario offers a tangible observational target. The rapid decay of these particles would have stirred the fabric of spacetime, producing a stochastic background of gravitational waves with characteristic frequencies in the nanohertz to millihertz range. Upcoming experiments such as the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) and the Pulsar Timing Array collaborations are poised to hunt for precisely such signals. Detecting a matching spectrum would not only lend credence to the sterile neutrino’s role in cosmic evolution but also open a new window onto physics beyond the Standard Model.

Skepticism remains, however. Critics point out that the model requires fine‑tuning of the sterile neutrino’s mass and mixing parameters to achieve the observed matter‑antimatter imbalance without conflicting with constraints from big‑bang nucleosynthesis and cosmic microwave background measurements. Moreover, alternative baryogenesis mechanisms – including electroweak baryogenesis and axion‑driven scenarios – continue to compete for theoretical favor. The authors acknowledge these challenges and stress that their proposal is intended as a proof‑of‑concept that revives a particle once thought irrelevant.

If future gravitational‑wave observatories confirm the predicted signal, the sterile neutrino could ascend from a footnote to a cornerstone of cosmology, reshaping our understanding of the universe’s earliest moments. Even a null result would be valuable, narrowing the parameter space for viable new physics and guiding the next generation of experiments. In either case, the renewed focus on this forgotten particle underscores how revisiting overlooked ideas can illuminate fundamental mysteries, reminding the scientific community that the answers to the cosmos may sometimes lie in the shadows of past theories.
